## TL;DR

The Remote runners panel’s primary status could mislead operators: a host at full capacity still read “ready,” and a reachable host with a failed latest run also read “ready.” I updated the headline state to identify fully occupied hosts as “busy” and surface the latest failed run as “last run failed.” Added a focused regression test for ready, busy, unreachable, and failing states. Headless WebKit QA at desktop and phone widths found no horizontal overflow or browser errors. The QA record is in `docs/qa/2026-11-remote-runners.md`.

## Work and rationale

I began by reading the task and the UI conventions, then inspected the Remote runners component, the Checks view, and its existing tests. The markup already exposed capacity, queued work, reachability, recent result, server statistics, and explanatory details. The missing piece was the headline state: it only reflected whether a host probe had succeeded. That made “ready” inaccurate for a full host and made a failed latest run visually secondary.

I adjusted the state resolver to preserve the existing priority of probe and reachability status, then report a failed latest run, then report full capacity, and finally report ready. The failure state is only selected for a reachable host; if it is unreachable, the user needs to see that immediate condition instead. The busy state is based on the advertised concurrency limit, so a host that still has one free slot can remain ready. Busy receives an amber treatment; a failed latest run receives a red treatment. The accessible text carries the full meaning, with the glyph serving as a visual cue.

The test mounts the panel with four representative host records and asserts the exact headline and class for each. It also asserts that a busy runner still shows its in-flight count and that the failed runner’s detail still says the last run failed. This protects both the new summary and the contextual information operators use to decide what to do.

For hands-on QA, I started the auth-less app with `just serve-noauth 7273` from a detached scratch worktree and used headless WebKit. The status endpoint was intercepted with synthetic data so all four states could be observed in one page without relying on actual runner availability. I tested 1280×1000 and 375×1000 viewports. At both widths, the document and body stayed within the viewport width, the rows showed the expected states, and the browser reported no page or console errors. I separately aborted the status request and observed the existing actionable “Can't reach the RepoOS server” message with no host rows. Since that path already identified the server as unreachable and instructed the user to restart it and reload, I left its behavior unchanged.

The QA note explicitly labels the runner data as synthetic. It does not claim that any real runner was contacted or measured. The note records the responsive results, the request failure observation, and the status discrepancy that prompted the change.

## Approaches tried

First I inspected the existing component and tests before changing anything. The component already had clear detail rows, including “Last completed,” “Running now,” queue position, memory health, and server stats. Adding another detailed warning section would have duplicated information. Updating the compact health headline was the smallest change that made the states scan correctly.

I then ran the app in a scratch worktree and intercepted its status endpoint in Playwright. The initial rendered page confirmed that an at-capacity host said “ready” despite showing `1/1 in flight`; a failed recent run likewise said “ready” while “Last completed” contained the failure. This confirmed the exact mismatch in the live rendering rather than relying on source inspection alone.

After implementing the resolver and test, I applied the same source diff to the scratch worktree, rebuilt it, and repeated the browser pass. The final rendered page showed “ready,” “busy,” “unreachable,” and “last run failed” as intended at both widths. I also ran the panel test file, which passed in both passes of the repository’s test wrapper.

## Challenges and blockers

No implementation blocker remained. The endpoint failure state did not need a code change: a deliberately aborted request showed the existing server-reachability message and gave a direct recovery action. Real runner health was not part of this pass; the host states were synthetic fixtures supplied to the browser. No real runner credentials or access were used.

The panel’s responsive rows contain many operational values, so the viewport pass checked document and body widths as well as whether the status details remained present. The narrow viewport did not create horizontal overflow. The app’s persistent mobile navigation overlays part of the scroll viewport by design; the runner panel itself remained scrollable, and no horizontal layout correction was needed.

## Key learnings

For a runner pool, “healthy” and “ready to accept work” are different facts. The probe tells us whether the host is reachable and usable; the in-flight count tells us whether it has capacity. The headline now reflects both without hiding the queue details. A recent failure also deserves a concise summary at the top of the host card, while the detailed “Last completed” row remains the place for task id, duration, and time.

Using a synthetic API response against the actual auth-less app let the QA pass exercise the whole rendered page consistently and safely. It provided evidence for the UI and responsive layout without turning a test into a claim about external hosts. The separate aborted-request check also confirmed that initial fetch failures already have a user-facing recovery message, so a redundant error presentation would have added noise.
